source.title: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon-AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap
source.authors: Catherine Li; Jing-Chu Gai; Andrej Risteski; Jacob Mitchell Springer; Aditi Raghunathan

record.tranche_reason: The study compares pretraining and fine-tuning outcomes for Muon and AdamW, but does not fit or test power laws, extrapolate losses from smaller runs, test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or assess the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out pretraining-loss comparisons across model sizes and token budgets, recorded under fits_no_version. Its fine-tuning frontiers, forgetting measures, and margin-to-spread results do not test the listed scaling-law versions. Scaling-law results cited from other work are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study compares Muon and AdamW base models after fine-tuning: learning–forgetting frontiers, crossover TPR and margin-to-spread ratio. It reports held-out pretraining loss across 30M–600M models and 5–2,560 TPR (Fig. 9, Fig. 3b), but fits no power law and makes no extrapolation. It does not test compute-optimal allocation or shape effects, and reports no downstream benchmark scaling. Hoffmann et al. is cited only to place TPR=20 as the compute-optimal reference. Its claim that pretraining loss is a poor proxy for adaptability is a cross-optimizer comparison of a fine-tuning learning–forgetting tradeoff. That is not V6's predictability of downstream task performance from scale or loss, so it is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that beyond a crossover pretraining budget AdamW beats Muon after fine-tuning, despite Muon's lower pretraining loss, and that the crossover falls with model size. They explain this with the margin-to-spread ratio and a one-step linear associative memory theorem.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares optimizer-dependent pretraining and fine-tuning outcomes rather than reproducing a scaling-law fitting or compute-allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported optimizer comparison varies with pretraining data budget and model size; the paper does not test sensitivity of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation to fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Muon reaches lower held-out DCLM pretraining loss than AdamW at every tested size and budget. The advantage shrinks with model size at 40 TPR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In OLMo-style 30M–600M runs, Muon's pretraining-loss advantage over AdamW shrinks as model size grows.

fits_no_version.finding: Muon has lower pretraining loss yet a worse learning–forgetting frontier beyond a crossover TPR. That crossover falls with model size, e.g. StackMathQA 320 TPR at 30M vs 10 TPR at 600M (Fig. 2, Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across pretraining optimizers, lower pretraining loss does not predict a better post-fine-tuning learning–forgetting tradeoff, increasingly so as the data budget grows.

record.problems: The relevant pretraining-loss comparisons are not presented as power-law fits or numerical extrapolation tests; the stated cross-size trend is not accompanied by numeric values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Fine-tuning frontier, forgetting, and margin-to-spread results were left out because they do not measure a behavior named by the claim versions. Cited scaling-law findings from other work were also excluded.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Loss curves vs TPR (Fig. 9) are shown without a functional-form test.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation analysis; TPR=20 is cited from Hoffmann et al.
No variation of depth or width at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in fine-tuning or other regimes.
No downstream benchmark performance measured as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents, so their dependence on optimizer or fitting choices is not tested. The optimizer-dependent pretraining-loss gap is not expressed as an exponent difference.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not a scaling-law study. The pretraining-loss-vs-adaptability result could interest a curator working on a 'loss as proxy' claim, but it does not bear on V6 as worded.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute; bottleneck conditions; several-orders-of-magnitude law.
Extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation trends.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and deviations from a single power law.
